Classical mechanics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 82k Articles: 1k
Classical mechanics describes the motion of bodies by assigning positions and velocities and specifying how their interactions change those quantities. A point mass is the simplest model: its size and internal structure are ignored, leaving a mass and a moving position. A rigid body retains orientation and rotational kinetic energy. Choosing a model means deciding which features affect the question being asked; a sliding block may be treated as a point mass, whereas predicting its rolling without slipping requires its moment of inertia.
Three complementary questions organize the subject. Newton's second law asks how the net force determines the instantaneous acceleration. The work-energy theorem asks how that force, acting through a displacement, changes kinetic energy. Conservation of mechanical energy asks which combinations of position and velocity are accessible when the interactions admit a time-independent potential energy and no other force supplies net power. These descriptions are compatible, but answer different questions: an energy calculation may find a maximum speed without first solving for position at every time.
The harmonic oscillator below makes this unity visible. A restoring force produces a repeating position trace; the corresponding phase plane has a closed ellipse; kinetic energy and potential energy exchange while their sum stays fixed. Lagrangian mechanics and Hamiltonian mechanics provide further ways to organize the same dynamics, especially when coordinates or constraints make individual forces awkward to track.
The scope of classical mechanics also matters. Newtonian mechanics approximates motion at speeds small compared with the speed of light; special relativity changes that description when this approximation fails. Quantum mechanics is needed for phenomena for which a classical assignment of simultaneous position and momentum is inadequate. These limitations do not prevent classical mechanics from being a useful predictive model within its regime. [ref]

Simple machine

Words: 117 Articles: 6
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
A mechanism that trades the magnitude or direction of an applied force against the displacement through which it acts. An ideal simple machine conserves work; it does not multiply energy.

Lever

Words: 57 Articles: 4
Simple machine OurBigBook.com
A body turning about a fulcrum. In static balance, effort and load supply equal and opposite torques: EdE​=LdL​, where the distances are perpendicular lever arms. Its ideal mechanical advantage is L/E=dE​/dL​. Measuring distances along the body instead of perpendicular to the force lines can give the wrong answer.

Fulcrum

Words: 8
Lever OurBigBook.com
The support or pivot about which a lever turns.

Mechanical advantage (MA=Fload​/Feffort​)

Words: 33
Simple machine OurBigBook.com
The ratio of the useful load force to the applied effort force. For an ideal simple machine in slow motion, the ratio of effort displacement to load displacement gives the same number by conservation of work.

Mechanical system

Words: 36
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
A collection of bodies and specified interactions whose configuration, velocities and evolution are studied in mechanics. Generalized coordinates describe its allowed configurations, while constraints restrict them. A model must specify which bodies and surroundings are included before applying conservation of momentum or conservation of energy.

Pulley

Words: 55
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
A wheel guiding a rope or cable so that it can redirect a tension force. An ideal fixed pulley changes the force direction without multiplying its magnitude. A freely rotating pulley with negligible moment of inertia and friction has equal rope tensions on its two sides; a finite moment of inertia instead relates their difference to its angular acceleration through the net torque.

Bead on a uniformly rotating wire ((1+f′2)r¨=ω2r−gf′−f′f′′r˙2)

Words: 95
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
A smooth wire has instantaneous shape z=f(r) in cylindrical coordinates and rotates at constant angular velocity θ˙=ω. The tangent vector at fixed time is er​+f′(r)ez​. Its dot product with the constraint force vanishes. Projecting Newton's second law along this tangent vector gives the equation in the title.
Multiplying that equation by r˙ proves conservation of
H=21​(1+f′(r)2)r˙2+U(r),U(r)=gf(r)−21​ω2r2.
(1)
This is a conserved quantity in the rotating description; the motor can exchange ordinary mechanical energy with the bead. A relative equilibrium at a>0 satisfies U′(a)=gf′(a)−ω2a=0. Its linearized equation is (1+f′(a)2)ϵ¨=−U′′(a)ϵ. A strict local minimum with U′′(a)>0 gives Lyapunov stability, while U′′(a)<0 gives an unstable equilibrium. If U′′(a)=0, higher orders are needed.

Deflection angle (δ)

Words: 55
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
For a trajectory with incoming and outgoing straight asymptotes, the deflection angle is the angle between its limiting incoming and outgoing velocity directions. For an attractive hyperbolic orbit of eccentricity e and impact parameter d, sin(δ/2)=1/e and tan(δ/2)=GM/(dv2), where v is the incoming speed at infinity. The incoming velocity points opposite to the incoming radial direction; ignoring that reversal gives the wrong angle.

Kinematics

Words: 149 Articles: 3
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
The description of motion through position, velocity and acceleration, before specifying the forces responsible. For constant acceleration these are related by integrating time derivatives. Projectile motion under an approximately uniform gravitational acceleration is an elementary example.

Relative motion

Words: 107 Articles: 1
Kinematics OurBigBook.com
The position and velocity of one body relative to another are the differences of their corresponding vectors in the same reference frame. Constant relative velocity gives an affine function of time, even when neither body is at rest.

Closest approach of two uniformly moving particles (t∗​=−d0​⋅v/∣v∣2)

Words: 72
Relative motion OurBigBook.com
If the relative position is d(t)=d0​+tv with v=0, completing the square gives
∣d(t)∣2=∣v∣2(t−t∗​)2+∣d0​∣2−∣v∣2(d0​⋅v)2​,t∗​=−∣v∣2d0​⋅v​.
(2)
This proves the minimum distance over all real times. If time is restricted to an interval, project t∗​ onto that interval; if v=0, the distance is constant. Both particles are evaluated at the same time, unlike the two independent parameters in the distance between skew lines.

Motion

Words: 9
Kinematics OurBigBook.com
Change of position with time relative to a specified reference system.

Near-surface recoil height with constant downward thrust

Words: 47
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
With upward initial speed v and a constant downward force F on remaining mass M, the near-surface excursion is H=v2/[2(g+F/M)]. A spherical body's surface gravity can be inferred from its escape speed: g=vesc2​/(2R). The approximation needs H≪R and no additional tether constraint.

Contact loss on a smooth sphere

Words: 38
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
A particle released from an infinitesimal displacement near the top of a smooth sphere has v2=2gR(1−cosθ). The normal reaction vanishes when mgcosθ=mv2/R, giving cosθ=2/3. The travelled arc is Rarccos(2/3), whereas the vertical drop is R/3.

Coulomb orbit

Words: 145 Articles: 2
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
A classical two-body trajectory in an inverse-distance Coulomb potential. With an effectively fixed centre and coupling C, a circular orbit has v2=C/(mr) and mechanical energy −C/(2r).

Coulomb head-on closest approach with target recoil (rmin​=ke​q1​q2​(m1​+m2​)/(m2​Klab​))

Words: 73
Coulomb orbit OurBigBook.com
A projectile of mass m1​, electric charge q1​, and nonrelativistic laboratory kinetic energy Klab​ approaches an initially stationary free target of mass m2​ and like-sign electric charge q2​. The relative-motion kinetic energy is K∗​=m2​Klab​/(m1​+m2​). At a head-on turning point it is converted to the repulsive Coulomb potential ke​q1​q2​/rmin​, proving the displayed separation. The remaining laboratory kinetic energy is the translation of the centre of mass; it cannot be converted into the pair's separation energy. An externally fixed target is the infinite-target-mass limit.

Classical radiation collapse of a Coulomb orbit

Words: 45
Coulomb orbit OurBigBook.com
An accelerating classical charge radiates according to the Larmor formula. For a slowly evolving nonrelativistic circular electron orbit, energy balance gives d(r3)/dt=−4cr02​, with r0​ the classical electron radius. The finite formal collapse time exposes classical atomic instability; it is not a model of a stable quantum atom.

Projectile motion

Words: 465 Articles: 7
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
Motion after launch under a specified gravitational field, with negligible drag force and no thrust. In a constant downward gravitational acceleration g, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical position obeys y(t)=y0​+vy0​t−gt2/2. Eliminating time gives a parabola when horizontal velocity is nonzero. Over larger distances the changing direction and magnitude of gravity require an orbital model instead.

Projectile

Words: 22
Projectile motion OurBigBook.com
An object launched into motion whose subsequent trajectory is determined by external forces. The ideal elementary projectile motion model retains uniform gravity and neglects air resistance.

Projectile range (R)

Words: 181 Articles: 2
Projectile motion OurBigBook.com
The horizontal displacement between launch and landing in a projectile motion model. With equal launch and landing heights, uniform gravitational acceleration g, no air resistance, launch speed u and angle θ, it is R=u2sin(2θ)/g. Different landing heights or forces change the result.

Maximum projectile range from an elevated launch (Xmax​=uu2+2gh​/g)

Words: 49
Projectile range OurBigBook.com
Under uniform gravity without drag, a projectile launched at speed u from height h reaches a maximum horizontal projectile range uu2+2gh​/g. For horizontal position X, maximize y=h+Xz−gX2(1+z2)/(2u2) over z=tanα. The maximizer is z=u2/(gX) and its envelope meets the ground at the displayed distance. The optimum angle obeys tanα=u/u2+2gh​.

Projectile range under a ceiling (Rmax​=8H(u2/g−2H)​if H≤u2/(4g))

Words: 92
Projectile range OurBigBook.com
A projectile launched from and returning to the floor beneath a horizontal ceiling of height H has maximum projectile range 8H(u2/g−2H)​ when 0≤H≤u2/(4g). For higher ceilings the maximum is u2/g. This assumes uniform gravitational acceleration, no air resistance and fixed launch speed u.
Indeed, with z=sin2θ, the apex condition is z≤2gH/u2 and R2=4u4z(1−z)/g2. This concave quadratic function is maximized at the admissible value nearest 1/2. Thus the lower-ceiling expression must not be extrapolated past its regime. If touching the ceiling is excluded, the limiting value is a supremum instead of an attained maximum.

Apex-target condition for a ballistic jet (uy​=2gh​,ux​=wg/(2h)​)

Words: 129 Articles: 1
Projectile motion OurBigBook.com
For a jet arriving horizontally at a target displaced horizontally by w and upward by h, the target lies at the projectile apex. Vertical kinematics gives uy2​=2gh and flight time uy​/g; the horizontal travel then fixes the displayed ux​. The launch speed is ux2​+uy2​​ and tanθ=2h/w. The ideal ballistic approximation neglects air drag, breakup and internal jet stresses after launch.

Jet-area adjustment during ballistic slowing (Ahit​vhit​=A0​u0​)

Words: 67
Apex-target condition for a ballistic jet OurBigBook.com
Steady incompressible mass flow rate stays constant along a jet, while speed and cross-sectional area can change under gravity. At a horizontal apex the arriving speed is the initial horizontal component. The force on a target that stops this horizontal momentum is m˙vhit​, using the conserved nozzle mass flux. Substituting the nozzle area into ρAhit​vhit2​ without adjusting the area gives the wrong result.

Ballistic orbit insertion with constant gravity (hb​=ho​−vo2​tan2θ/(2g))

Words: 83
Projectile motion OurBigBook.com
In the flat-surface, constant-gravitational acceleration model, a coasting projectile conserves horizontal velocity. If it arrives at the top of its trajectory with horizontal speed vo​, its earlier velocity at angle θ above the horizontal has vertical component vo​tanθ. Static friction supplies the force needed to maintain rest, up to its bound; kinetic friction has a prescribed magnitude in the ideal constant-coefficient model. Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
Inertia is a body's persistence in its state of rest or constant velocity when the net external force vanishes in an inertial frame. It is not an extra force that pushes a moving body forward. Newton's first law describes this persistence; for a point mass, Newton's second law quantifies how a nonzero net external force changes its momentum. At constant mass, Fnet​=ma, so a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration for the same net force.
A moving cart does not need a forward net force to maintain its velocity. Ordinary carts slow because friction and drag force produce an opposing net external force; reducing those interactions reveals Newton's first law more clearly. The air-track test of inertial motion separates this persistence from the initial push. In overdamped particle dynamics, the inertial acceleration term is small compared with drag force over the time scales considered; that approximation does not mean that inertia has disappeared.

Torsion balance

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Classical mechanics OurBigBook.com
A torsion balance measures a weak torque by suspending a body from a thin fiber and reading its twist angle. The fiber supports the body's gravitational weight while permitting rotation about the suspension axis. In the range of linear elasticity, a twist θ in radians, measured from the untwisted reference orientation, produces a restoring torque
τfiber​=−κθ,κ>0.
(10)
The torsion constant κ sets the sensitivity. At static equilibrium with an applied torque τext​ and no other axial torque, τext​=κθ. A perpendicular force F at lever arm a therefore gives θ=aF/κ. The torsion balance measures a turning effect: a force whose line of action passes through the suspension axis gives no axial torque. The Cavendish torsion balance is the gravitational application; Coulomb's law supplies an electrical one. [ref]
The original schematic separates two ways of reading the same torque. In deflection operation the top attachment stays fixed and the body rotates. In null operation the experimenter rotates the top attachment by α while returning the body's laboratory angle β to its original value. If the initially untwisted configuration has α=β=0, the fiber twist is θ=β−α, not β alone. Thus
τfiber​=−κ(β−α),τext​=κ(β−α).
(11)
For a positive applied torque, holding β=0 requires α=−τext​/κ. Keeping the body at the same angle keeps the lever arm and source geometry fixed, making comparison of different applied forces easier. Either readout still requires a calibrated torsion constant and a stable reference orientation.
An illustrative calculation shows the amplification: with a=0.050m, F=2.0×10−9N, and κ=1.0×10−8Nm/rad, the applied torque is 1.0×10−10Nm and the equilibrium twist is 0.010rad≃0.573∘. These are stipulated values, not measured data. Reducing the torsion constant tenfold increases this twist tenfold, provided the fiber remains in its calibrated linear elasticity range. The cost is a slower response, explained by the oscillation period in torsion constant.
A concrete laboratory experiment is PASCO's Coulomb balance: level its counterbalanced rod, discharge both conducting spheres, and set the unloaded zero. Charge the spheres at maximum separation; switch off the charging supply. Move the second sphere to a known center separation R, then turn the suspension dial until the rod returns to its index mark. Record the dial change and R, recharge, and repeat at several separations. The manual recommends a draft-free room, clean insulating supports, and recharging before each reading: leakage, especially in humid conditions, otherwise changes the electric charges during the sequence. At close separations the conducting spheres redistribute charge, so the point charge approximation needs correction. [ref]
For constant electric charges and a fixed perpendicular lever arm, the Coulomb's law prediction is ∣θ∣∝R−2. Plotting the logarithm of twist magnitude against the logarithm of separation gives log∣θ∣=constant−2logR, so the predicted slope is −2. Absolute force measurement additionally needs the torsion constant; comparing ratios can eliminate it if it remains stable. Repeating a reference separation between other settings distinguishes a separation effect from a changing signal. A declining reading at the reference separation would invalidate the assumption of unchanged electric charges, even if a distance plot looks smooth.
The historical electrical example is Coulomb's first memoir of 1785. His apparatus enclosed a suspended needle with a small ball and a second ball; an adjustable head twisted the suspension. After charging the balls by contact, he reported angular separations 36∘, 18∘, and 8.5∘ with head settings 0∘, 126∘, and 567∘. The total twists were approximately 36∘, 144∘, and 576∘: fourfold restoring torque accompanied approximately halved separation. These are his reported observations, not data from our diagrams. [ref] A precise reconstruction must use center distances and the changing lever arm, rather than identify angular separation exactly with distance; Alberto A. Martínez's replication explicitly analyzes that geometry. [ref]
Sensitivity also exposes changes of the apparatus itself. Fleischer and colleagues' cryogenic torsion balance used a temperature-controlled enclosure to reduce vacuum-vessel top-plate temperature fluctuations to approximately ±0.01K, limiting changes in suspension geometry from thermal expansion. They used a mild bake-out near 40∘C to speed initial fiber relaxation and reduce slow zero motion. Their optical readout compared the pendulum mirror with an internal reference mirror to reject shared optical motion. Room-temperature thermal radiation entering through the optical opening heated the pendulum; a cold filter reduced that load. The authors could not directly measure the pendulum's temperature without disturbing it, and explicitly distinguished the cold shield's temperature from the body's. Cooling therefore requires checking the actual noise and thermal environment, rather than assuming that the fiber and body share the shield's temperature. [ref]
A useful control strategy is to record unloaded readings and temperature before and after each signal sequence, recalibrate the torsion constant under the same conditions, and compare forward and reverse settings. The algebra of torsion balance zero drift shows precisely which offsets such comparisons can cancel. A fine angular scale alone does not establish a small measurement error.

PASCO's procedure turns the Coulomb balance on its side and adds small known masses to generate a gravitational weight at the sphere's lever arm, returning the rod to its index mark by turning the dial. Its tabulated coefficient is force per degree: multiply by the lever arm and 180/π to obtain our torsion constant. [ref]
The figure's ideal static calibration uses κ=1.0×10−8Nm/rad: an applied torque of 2.0×10−10Nm gives 0.020rad. Both signs lie on the same straight line. The plotted points are calculated examples, not experimental observations; they cannot demonstrate a real fiber's linearity.
Dynamic calibration instead measures the oscillation period T0​ with known total suspended moment of inertia I. For negligible damping, small free oscillations about a fixed reference obey simple harmonic motion:
Iθ¨+κθ=0,T0​=2πκI​​,κ=T02​4π2I​.
(15)
Include the rod, mirrors, and any attachments in I unless their contributions are demonstrably negligible. Keep the applied torque absent or independent of angle. If an external torque has derivative gτ​=dτext​/dθ at equilibrium, linearization gives effective stiffness κ−gτ​: timing alone then measures that combination, and stability requires κ−gτ​>0. A constant applied torque merely shifts equilibrium. Non-negligible damping changes the measured period; damped torsional oscillation gives a correction under a specified damping model. Agreement between static and dynamic calibrations is a useful check on the assumed moment of inertia, reference stability, and restoring law, rather than a reason to ignore their assumptions.

In the ideal viscous model, damping contributes −bθ˙ with constant b≥0. This is a rotational damped harmonic oscillator. For known constant moment of inertia I and torsion constant κ, define γ=b/(2I). In the oscillatory regime γ2<κ/I,

These equations assume a single rotational mode, a stationary zero, linear elasticity, and viscous damping. For two equal and opposite applied torques measured at the same reference zero, their equilibrium angles differ by 2τext​/κ. A stable offset cancels; a changing zero contributes β0​(t+​)−β0​(t−​) and does not cancel automatically.
A simple symmetric sequence makes the limitation explicit. Let b1​,b2​,b3​ be settled equilibrium angles for applied torques +τ,−τ,+τ at equally spaced times t0​−h,t0​,t0​+h. If the unloaded zero is linear in time, β0​(t)=u+vt, and κ and τ remain fixed, then

The virial theorem relates the average value of a function along a trajectory to the forces that bind it. For an isolated system of particles interacting through Newtonian gravitational potential energy, it gives 2⟨K⟩+⟨U⟩=0: the average kinetic energy is half the magnitude of the average negative potential energy. An eccentric Kepler orbit makes the distinction vivid: kinetic energy and potential energy vary throughout the orbit, although their sum is constant. The relation concerns their time averages, rather than their values at every instant. It underlies the virial mass estimate and the negative heat capacity of a virialized gravitational system.
Use constant positive particle masses mi​, positions ri​, mechanical momenta pi​=mi​r˙i​, and total kinetic energy K=∑i​pi2​/(2mi​). The auxiliary quantity G(t) is a sum of dot products, not the gravitational constant, which we denote here by GN​:
G(t)=∑i​pi​(t)⋅ri​(t),⟨A⟩T​=T1​∫0T​A(t)dt,2⟨K⟩T​+⟨∑i​ri​⋅Fi​⟩T​=TG(T)−G(0)​.
(32)
This finite-T identity is exact wherever Newton's second law holds along a regular trajectory; Fi​ must include every force. The endpoint term is what a finite observation window leaves behind. For the infinite-time theorem, suppose the averages on the left exist and (G(T)−G(0))/T→0. A sufficient condition is uniformly bounded positions and velocities for finitely many particles. More generally G(T)=o(T) suffices, even without those individual bounds. Bounded positions alone do not supply a bound on momenta, especially near a singular potential energy; nor does a small endpoint term prove thermodynamic equilibrium. Periodic motion with G(T)=G(0) gives the identity without an endpoint term at that finite T. For an isolated system, use an inertial centre of mass frame so translational drift does not contribute bulk kinetic energy.[ref]
For a differentiable potential energy that is a homogeneous function of degree q, choose its additive constant so that the scaling law really holds. With conservative forces, the Euler theorem for homogeneous functions gives
U(λr1​,…,λrN​)=λqU(r1​,…,rN​),∑i​ri​⋅Fi​=−qU,2⟨K⟩T​−q⟨U⟩T​=TG(T)−G(0)​.
(33)
Thus a harmonic oscillator has q=2 and ⟨K⟩=⟨U⟩. An isolated system with Newtonian gravitational potential energy has
U=−GN​∑i<j​∣ri​−rj​∣mi​mj​​,q=−1,2⟨K⟩+⟨U⟩=0,E=⟨K⟩+⟨U⟩=−⟨K⟩.
(34)
Each interacting pair occurs once, and U=0 at infinite separation. Here the total energy E=K+U is conserved. An external field or a mixture of different scaling powers requires its own force term; one cannot assign the whole potential energy a single degree q. The virial theorem for a homogeneous pair potential states the corresponding general energy relation.

Equivalently, for the scalar inertia I=21​∑i​mi​∣ri​∣2 used in the pairwise moment-of-inertia identity, I˙=G and I¨=2K+∑i​ri​⋅Fi​. Specifying this factor of one half avoids confusion with another common inertia convention.
In On a Mechanical Theorem applicable to Heat by R. Clausius (1870, pp. 123-124), the author defines stationary motion through bounded positions and velocities, includes planetary orbits and elastic vibrations, and names the average negative half of the force-position sum the “virial”. That historical convention differs from the auxiliary G(t) defined above. His proof on pp. 126-127 keeps an endpoint term, then explains why it vanishes over a complete period or becomes small in a long bounded irregular motion. The same paper separates internal and external forces and includes uniform boundary pressure on pp. 125-126: confinement was already part of the formulation, rather than a reason to omit external stresses.[ref]

Simple harmonic motion is motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and points back towards it:
x¨=−ω2x,ω>0.
(40)
Here x is measured from equilibrium, and ω is the constant angular frequency. For a point mass attached to an ideal spring, Hooke's law gives the restoring force F=−kx, with stiffness k>0, and Newton's second law yields ω=k/m​. The minus sign matters: for x>0 the force is negative, and for x<0 it is positive. A restoring force need not oppose velocity; on the return towards equilibrium it increases speed.
The general solution is
x(t)=Acos(ωt+φ),v(t)=−Aωsin(ωt+φ),P=ω2π​.
(41)
The amplitude A≥0 and oscillation phase φ encode the initial conditions. We use P for the oscillation period to distinguish it from kinetic energy T. For A>0, the oscillation period is independent of amplitude, the property of isochronous harmonic motion. At A=0 the body remains at equilibrium. [ref]
Choose m=0.5kg, k=2N/m, and release the mass from rest at displacement A=0.3m. Then ω=2s−1, P=πs, and φ=0. Writing time t in seconds,
x(t)=0.3cos(2t)m,v(t)=−0.6sin(2t)m/s.
(42)
At t=0 the velocity vanishes, but the acceleration is −1.2m/s2: a turning point is not a state of rest that persists. At t=π/4s, the body crosses equilibrium with velocity −0.6m/s and zero acceleration. At t=π/2s it reaches the opposite turning point, x=−0.3m.
Taking potential energy zero at equilibrium, the same solution gives
V(t)=21​kx(t)2=0.09cos2(2t)J,T(t)=21​mv(t)2=0.09sin2(2t)J,E=T+V=0.09J.
(43)
At each turning point all mechanical energy is potential energy; at each equilibrium crossing it is kinetic energy. Both repeat twice during one complete position cycle because squaring removes the sign. At t=π/8s, for example, each contributes 0.045J.
The physical position trace covers a line segment, −0.3≤x≤0.3 in metres. In the phase plane, the paired position and velocity instead trace the ellipse

This is precisely mv2/2+kx2/2=E, rewritten: the single conserved mechanical energy fixes the amplitude and the whole ellipse. It does not fix the starting oscillation phase. At x=0 both v=−0.6m/s and v=+0.6m/s lie on it; position alone cannot distinguish them. Replacing v by momentum p=mv gives the equivalent phase-space trajectory. The arrows show increasing time, clockwise in (x,v) coordinates.
This closed ellipse assumes a time-independent spring and no damping or applied drive. Adding a resisting force −bv, b>0, gives mx¨+bx˙+kx=0 and dE/dt=−bv2≤0. An underdamped damped harmonic oscillator spirals inward in the phase plane, crossing successively smaller energy contours. The ideal harmonic oscillator is also useful beyond springs: near a smooth potential energy minimum with V′′(0)>0, its Taylor expansion begins with V(0)+V′′(0)x2/2. For sufficiently small displacements, this gives the same restoring force to leading order, explaining why small oscillations share one solvable pattern.

A particle of kinetic energy αmc2 hitting an equal mass at rest, with equal and opposite outgoing angles θ, obeys tanθ=2/(α+2)​. Conservation of total energy gives equal final energies, and longitudinal momentum conservation fixes the angle.

Elastic collision OurBigBook.com
A projectile of mass m1​ elastically scattering from a stationary target of mass m2​<m1​ has the displayed maximum laboratory angle. In c=1 units, let its incident energy be E>m1​ and s=m12​+m22​+2m2​E. Boosting the outgoing four-momentum from the center-of-momentum frame gives tanθ=sinφ/[Γ(cosφ+B)], with Γ=(E+m2​)/s​ and B=(m12​+m2​E)/[m2​(E+m2​)]>1. The maximum at cosφ=−1/B has tanθmax​=1/[ΓB2−1​]=m2​/m12​−m22​​. Equality is allowed; a strict upper bound would exclude a realizable outgoing direction. The angular cap is independent of incident energy.

Inelastic collision

Words: 241 Articles: 2
Collision mechanics OurBigBook.com
An inelastic collision changes total kinetic energy. In the dissipative case it decreases, transferring energy to internal energy, including deformation and microscopic motion. Isolated colliding bodies still obey momentum conservation; conservation of energy requires accounting for the transferred energy. Bodies need not stick in every inelastic collision. The decrease in translational kinetic energy drives dissipative spreading of a planetary ring.
For the incoming masses and velocities in the elastic collision example, stipulate that the bodies stick. This perfectly inelastic collision has a shared outgoing velocity
v=m1​+m2​m1​u1​+m2​u2​​=3kg6kgm/s​=2m/s.
(47)
The outgoing momenta are 4 and 2kgm/s, totaling 6kgm/s. The outgoing kinetic energies are 4 and 2J, totaling 6J. Thus 9−6=3J of kinetic energy becomes internal energy within the isolated pair. Nothing in momentum conservation requires this 3J to remain as kinetic energy. [ref]
Adhesive collision of two equal discs
Words: 83
Inelastic collision OurBigBook.com
Two uniform discs of mass m and radius a stick at first edge contact. One initially translates at speed v and the other rests, with neither initially spinning. If the incoming velocity makes angle θ to the line of centres, the composite axial moment of inertia about its centre of mass is 3ma2. Conserved angular-momentum magnitude is mav∣sinθ∣, so the angular velocity magnitude is v∣sinθ∣/(3a). The centre-of-mass speed is v/2. Splitting kinetic energy into translation and rotation gives Kf​=mv2(1/4+sin2θ/6). The difference from mv2/2 is dissipated internally; it cannot be removed from angular-momentum conservation.

Inelastic collision OurBigBook.com
A perfectly inelastic collision is an inelastic collision in which the bodies stick and share one outgoing velocity. For two isolated point masses, momentum conservation gives v=(m1​u1​+m2​u2​)/(m1​+m2​). At fixed total momentum, common velocity minimizes the outgoing translational kinetic energy, so sticking gives the greatest loss of that kinetic energy for the specified incoming state.

Oblique collision OurBigBook.com
In a smooth oblique collision, the impulse is parallel to the contact normal n, while tangential velocity components remain unchanged. Incoming velocities, masses, and a coefficient of restitution do not determine the outgoing velocities until that contact normal, or equivalent scattering data, is specified. For an elastic collision of masses 3m,m, incoming velocities (−u,0) and (3​w/2,w/2), and outgoing first velocity (0,h), conservation of momentum and conservation of kinetic energy give w(3​u+h)=2u2+4h2. Thus specifying only the first outgoing x component leaves a family: h=0 gives w=2u/3​, while h=u/3​ gives w=53​u/6.

Impulse (J)

Words: 389 Articles: 3
Collision mechanics OurBigBook.com
The impulse of a force over a time interval is its vector integral:
J=∫ti​tf​​F(t)dt.
(48)
Its International System of Units unit is Ns=kgm/s. The impulse-momentum theorem equates the net impulse to the change in momentum. For one fixed-mass point mass, integrate its net force; for a closed collection obeying Newton's third law, integrate the sum of external forces. In one dimension, the signed area under the force versus time graph gives the impulse; negative force contributes negative area. [ref]
Three stipulated rightward net force pulses illustrate the same J=6Ns: constant 12N for 0.5s, a triangle rising from zero to 24N at 0.25s and falling to zero at 0.5s, and constant 3N for 2s. Their areas are
(12N)(0.5s)=21​(24N)(0.5s)=(3N)(2s)=6Ns.
(49)
Applied separately to the same fixed mass m=2kg, each gives Δv=J/m=3m/s. Their peak forces differ: 12, 24, and 3N. Thus impulse fixes the final momentum change, while the force history determines how abruptly it occurs.
The mean net force over the chosen interval is F=J/(tf​−ti​). Extending the interval for a fixed impulse reduces this mean force. A lower peak force additionally depends on the pulse shape: the two short pulses above have the same mean 12N but different peaks. This explains why controlling the duration and shape of a stopping impulse matters in cushioning a collision.

Impulse OurBigBook.com
An impulse directed along the position vector relative to a specified origin. Its angular impulse vanishes because ΔJ=r×Δp=0. It can nevertheless change kinetic energy; if an initially circular Kepler orbit receives radial velocity w, the added specific orbital energy is w2/2.
Radial kick from a circular Kepler orbit (e=β−1​)
Words: 65
Radial impulse OurBigBook.com
A radial impulse that multiplies the initial circular kinetic energy by β>1 adds radial velocity ±GM/r0​​β−1​ and leaves specific angular momentum j2=GMr0​. The new specific orbital energy is GM(β−2)/(2r0​), yielding orbital eccentricity e=β−1​ and semilatus rectum p=r0​. For 1<β<2, the apsidal radii are r0​/(1±e); for β≥2 there is no finite apocentre. A nonzero radial kick occurs away from an apsis, so the old circular radius is not automatically the new periapsis.

For one fixed-mass point mass, this becomes Jnet​=Δp=mΔv. Zero external impulse implies equal initial and final total momenta; momentum conservation throughout the interval requires zero net external force throughout it.

Center of mass OurBigBook.com
For a closed system with fixed total mass, summing the constituent Newton's second law equations makes pairwise internal forces cancel when Newton's third law applies. The remaining resultant external force is the derivative of total momentum, equal to Mr¨CM​. This governs translation of the center of mass; external torque additionally governs changes of angular momentum.

The point through which the resultant gravitational force acts when that force has a single point of application. In a uniform gravitational field, it coincides with the center of mass; a nonuniform field need not give the same point.

For a solid cone of base radius a, height h and density ρ(r)=ρ0​(r/a)p, take p>−2 so the axis singularity, if present, is integrable. In cylindrical coordinates, at fixed radius r the vertical range is 0≤z≤h(1−r/a). Integrating over height first gives
Mp​=2πρ0​∫0a​(r/a)prh(1−r/a)dr=(p+2)(p+3)2πρ0​a2h​.
(52)
The first height moment is πρ0​∫0a​(r/a)prh2(1−r/a)2dr=2πρ0​a2h2/[(p+2)(p+3)(p+4)]. Dividing proves dp​=h/(p+4). Thus uniform density has centroid h/4, while density proportional to radius has centroid h/5. For sums of such density components, total masses and first moments add, giving a mass-weighted centroid.

Barycenter (astronomy)

Center of mass OurBigBook.com
The centre of mass of an astronomical system. In an isolated two-body problem, both bodies follow orbits around their shared astronomical barycenter; the Kepler orbit of their relative displacement has a semi-major axis equal to the sum of their individual semi-major axes.

Center of mass OurBigBook.com
Suppose a body of mass M0​ has centre of mass R0​, and material of mass Mc​<M0​ with centre of mass Rc​ is removed. Additivity of the first mass moment gives the remaining centre of mass
R=M0​−Mc​M0​R0​−Mc​Rc​​.
(53)
When the original centre of mass is at the origin, the remaining centre of mass points opposite the removed material's first mass moment. For a constrained rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, this displaced centre of mass undergoes centripetal acceleration even if the applied axial torque is zero.

The weighted relative velocities sum to zero, so expanding the kinetic energy eliminates the mixed term and yields the displayed decomposition. For a rigid body, the relative contribution is the rotational kinetic energy Iω2/2 about the chosen centre-of-mass axis.

α=q2​−q1​,β=q3​−q2​,γ=2π−q3​+q1​

and the collective angle Φ=(q1​+q2​+q3​)/3. Then α+β+γ=2π. For three equal masses on a circle of radius r,
T=23mr2​Φ˙2+3mr2​(α˙2+α˙β˙​+β˙​2).

Reduced mass (μ)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Center of mass OurBigBook.com
The reduced mass is the effective mass for the two-particle relative coordinate of two bodies with constant positive masses m1​,m2​:
μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​,μ1​=m1​1​+m2​1​.
(58)
Both bodies can respond to their mutual force, so their relative acceleration is greater than if one were fixed. Consequently 0<μ<min(m1​,m2​). This explains why using either individual mass, or their sum, generally gives the wrong internal oscillation rate. The same reduced mass describes a two-body problem, a free two-mass spring, and the approximate molecular vibration of a diatomic molecule.[ref]
For equal masses m1​=m2​=m, μ=m/2. Two 1kg bodies therefore have μ=0.5kg: in their stationary centre of mass frame a relative speed 2m/s means individual speeds 1m/s and total kinetic energy 1J. With m1​=1kg and m2​=100kg, instead μ=100/101kg≈0.990099kg. At the same relative speed, the individual speeds are 200/101 and 2/101m/s, and the total kinetic energy is 200/101J. These are calculations for stipulated masses and velocities.
For fixed m1​ and q=m2​/m1​>0, μ/m1​=q/(1+q). The heavy-partner limit q→∞ gives μ→m1​ from below; the relative error incurred by replacing μ with m1​ is (m1​−μ)/μ=1/q. At q=100 this is 1%. Treating the heavy body as fixed is thus a controlled approximation to internal motion, rather than an exact consequence of its being heavier.

Two-particle relative coordinate (r=r2​−r1​)

Words: 300
Reduced mass OurBigBook.com
Choose positions in one inertial frame and let M=m1​+m2​. The centre of mass and two-particle relative coordinate are
R=Mm1​r1​+m2​r2​​,r=r2​−r1​,r1​=R−Mm2​​r,r2​=R+Mm1​​r.
(59)
The lighter body is farther from the centre of mass. Reconstructing both positions from these equations is part of solving the two-body problem; r alone describes their separation, not either body's laboratory position.[ref]
Substitute the reconstructed velocities into the kinetic energy. The result is the exact two-particle instance of kinetic-energy decomposition about the centre of mass:
T=21​m1​∣r˙1​∣2+21​m2​∣r˙2​∣2=21​M∣R˙∣2+21​μ∣r˙∣2.
(60)
The mixed dot product has coefficient −m1​m2​/M+m2​m1​/M=0; the coefficient of ∣r˙∣2 is (m1​m22​+m2​m12​)/M2=μ. This algebra needs constant positive masses but no particular force law. In the stationary centre of mass frame, the fraction of internal kinetic energy carried by body 1 is m2​/M, and by body 2 is m1​/M: the lighter body carries more.
For a closed pair with no external forces, write F for the force on body 2 and −F for that on body 1, as required by Newton's third law. Adding and subtracting their Newton's second law equations yields
MR¨=0,r¨=(m2​1​+m1​1​)F,μr¨=F.
(61)
Thus the centre of mass moves uniformly while the two-particle relative coordinate behaves like one body of reduced mass. Equal-opposite internal forces suffice for these equations. For an internal central force, F=f(r)r with r=∣r∣>0, the internal torque vanishes and conservation of angular momentum gives constant Lrel​=μr×r˙. If the central force comes from a time-independent potential energy U(r), then f(r)=−dU/dr and the internal mechanical energy Erel​=μ∣r˙∣2/2+U(r) is conserved. The kinetic energy split alone does not establish either conservation law.

Free two-mass spring (ω=k/μ​)

Words: 197
Reduced mass OurBigBook.com
Take two point masses joined by a massless spring of spring constant k>0 and equilibrium length ℓ>0. Assume one-dimensional motion along the spring, no external force, no damping, and an extension s=x2​−x1​−ℓ satisfying Hooke's law; keep x2​>x1​. For a real spring this is a model within its elastic range. Its potential energy is U=ks2/2, so
μs¨=−ks,s(t)=Acos(ωt+ϕ),ω=μk​​=k(m1​1​+m2​1​)​,ν=2πω​.
(62)
Here ω is angular frequency and ν is frequency. Choose ∣A∣<ℓ so the model bodies do not cross. The internal normal mode has displacements u1​=−m2​s/M and u2​=m1​s/M about equilibrium offsets from the centre of mass; its amplitude ratio is ∣u1​∣/∣u2​∣=m2​/m1​. The other normal mode is collective translation with zero frequency and no spring extension. This free pair has different boundary conditions from normal modes of two equal masses between three springs.
For k=10N/m and two 1kg masses, ω=20​s−1≈4.47214s−1 and ν≈0.711763Hz. Replacing the second mass by 100kg gives ω=10.1​s−1≈3.17805s−1 and ν≈0.505802Hz. Fixing the second endpoint instead would give 10​s−1: the free heavy partner still moves. The free pair's angular frequency exceeds that fixed-end limit by the factor 1+1/q​, about 1.004988 at q=100.

Isotope scaling of diatomic vibration (ν′/ν≃μ/μ′​)

Words: 499 Articles: 1
Reduced mass OurBigBook.com
Near a stable equilibrium bond length re​, a Taylor expansion of a diatomic molecule's potential energy gives U(r)≃U(re​)+k(r−re​)2/2, with k=U′′(re​)>0. Treat the internal stretch as a harmonic oscillator of reduced mass, initially omitting molecular rotation. If replacing an isotope leaves this local potential energy curvature unchanged, then
νν′​≃μ′μ​​,νharm​=2πc1​μk​​.
(63)
Here c is the speed of light and νharm​ a spectroscopic wavenumber; use consistent length units for c and νharm​. The quantum harmonic oscillator gives adjacent energy eigenvalues separated by hν, with h the Planck constant. Consequently a vibrational photon absorption can probe the same frequency scale, subject to electric-dipole selection rules.
For an explicitly approximate isotope example, assign the atomic masses of 1H, 2H, 35Cl, and 37Cl the mass-number values 1u,2u,35u,37u, respectively, with u the unified atomic mass unit. These are stipulated approximations to individual atomic masses, not measured masses of molecules or natural-abundance averages. They give
μH35Cl​=3635​u,μD35Cl​=3770​u,νH35Cl​νD35Cl​​≃7237​​≈0.716860,νH35Cl​νH37Cl​​≃666665​​≈0.999249.
(64)
The symbol D means deuterium, 2H. Doubling the light partner's approximate atomic mass therefore produces a large predicted shift, whereas changing the already heavy chlorine partner by two mass units produces a much smaller one. A quantitative comparison with infrared spectroscopy requires actual isotope-specific atomic masses, fitted band parameters, and uncertainties, rather than identifying any arbitrary peak with νharm​.
HCl and DCl vibrational isotope experiment
Words: 305
Isotope scaling of diatomic vibration OurBigBook.com
An actual infrared spectroscopy route is to compare gaseous hydrogen chloride containing ordinary hydrogen with its deuterium counterpart. A documented teaching experiment uses a stopcock-equipped gas cell with potassium bromide windows and a Nicolet Avatar instrument for Fourier transform spectroscopy. A nitrogen-purged flask and drying tube supply the mixture; the sample also contains sulfur dioxide. An empty sample-chamber background precedes the filled-cell scan. The absorbance trace and peak-picked spectroscopic wavenumbers are the readout. The analysis assigns and indexes 1H35Cl and 2H35Cl transitions separately and propagates transition uncertainties. The instructions distinguish resolvable chlorine isotope peaks from adequate precision for the intended parameter analysis. [ref]
A separate published teaching dataset reports a Nicolet Nexus 670 instrument, a 10cm gas cell at 20Torr, and chlorine isotope peaks resolved to baseline. These apparatus details describe that dataset, not the preceding experiment. [ref]
The inference connects several models. Fit correctly assigned transitions to separate molecular rotation from molecular vibration, then compare the inferred vibrational scales using isotope scaling of diatomic vibration. Agreement supports the approximate separation between a nearly unchanged chemical bond stiffness and a changed nuclear mass. It does not make a real molecule an exact classical spring: anharmonicity shifts the fundamental transition away from the local harmonic oscillator scale, and coupling to molecular rotation shifts individual lines.
For an independent test, calculate the reduced masses from the specified isotopes and compare the inferred values k=μ(2πcνharm​)2. Agreement within uncertainty tests the common-curvature assumption; choosing separate k values just to fit each frequency would not test it. The documented background addresses instrument and ambient contributions, but does not by itself subtract window absorption, identify contaminating species, or calibrate the spectroscopic wavenumber scale. Those require separate controls. Finite spectral resolution, blended peaks, incorrect isotope assignments, and departure from the harmonic approximation near a potential minimum limit the comparison. No numerical measured line positions are assumed here.
